documents: The standardized data extraction form for the study is available from Review Manager (RevMan v.9.5.1) at https://revman.cochrane.org.
Data extracted from the included studies are provided in the manuscript.
The data used for all analyses of the semaglutide and NAION meta-analysis are available in the manuscript.
The code for reproducibility of the semaglutide and NAION meta-analysis is publicly available in Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17885011.
The systematic review searched the PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science databases for observational studies published from January 2023 to November 2025.
Pooled hazard ratios and 95% confidence intervals for the semaglutide and NAION meta-analysis were calculated using fixed-effects models.
Risk of bias for the semaglutide and NAION meta-analysis was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and ROBINS-I v.2.

The study included five eligible observational studies and seven additional studies for sensitivity analysis, with semaglutide use associated with a hazard ratio of 2.17 (95% CI [1.73, 2.74]) for nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy compared with nonsemaglutide glucose-lowering regimens.

The absolute risk of nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy in semaglutide-treated patients was 0.014% (95% CI [0.005%, 0.023%]), corresponding to approximately 1 additional case per 7,000 patients annually.
The evidence synthesis was limited to retrospective, registry-based observational studies, introducing potential biases from study-level outcome misclassification and confounding.

The study performed a meta-analysis of 5 primary longitudinal observational real-world studies and 7 additional studies for sensitivity analysis to determine the association between semaglutide therapy and NAION risk in patients with T2D.

The researchers compared their data with 2 meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials, 4 meta-analyses of observational studies, 9 systematic reviews, 2 consensus statements, and 4 regulatory communications.

The meta-analysis included studies relying on retrospective, registry-based designs that used International Classification of Diseases codes to identify nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) cases, introducing potential misclassification and confounding by indication. The overall certainty of evidence for these findings was graded as low to very low.

High-quality, prospective studies employing standardized diagnostic criteria for nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) are required to confirm the reported association between semaglutide and NAION.

Semaglutide functions as a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) and is associated with an increased risk of nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), with adjusted hazard ratios ranging from approximately 1.26 to 6.84 in patients with type 2 diabetes.

The incidence of nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) in the general population is approximately 3.89 to 10.19 cases per 100,000 patient-years, and the risk is particularly elevated in the first 12 months after semaglutide treatment initiation.

The umbrella review utilized the JBI Manual for Evidence Synthesis and PRISMA 2020 guidelines, with literature searches conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science from January 2023 to November 2025. Additional sources were identified through targeted grey literature searches and citation tracking of the World Health Organization, European Medicines Agency, and Food and Drug Administration.

Eligible publications for the umbrella review were required to use systematic methods for study identification, selection, or appraisal and examine ocular safety outcomes relevant to NAION in the context of semaglutide, GLP-1 RAs, or related agents. Commentaries and nonmethodological narrative summaries were excluded unless issued by regulatory agencies or professional societies.

Data extraction for the umbrella review used a structured form capturing review type, objective, population, intervention, comparators, included study designs, synthesis methods, and principal findings. Methodological quality was appraised using the AMSTAR 2 tool by two reviewers, with discrepancies resolved by consensus, and no quantitative pooling was performed due to heterogeneity in scope, analytical approaches, and outcome definitions.

The study selection process identified 218 records across three databases, which reduced to 95 records after duplicate removal and 38 full-text reports after screening. The 38 full-text reports consisted of 20 for the meta-analysis and 18 for the umbrella review.

The systematic review and meta-analysis was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) under number CRD420251025896 with further amendments. The review followed Methodological Expectations of Cochrane Intervention Reviews (MECIR) standards and reported results in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines.

A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science databases for studies published between January 2023 and April 2025, with a repeat search including studies published through November 2025. The search strategy combined Medical Subject Headings and keywords related to semaglutide, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and NAION, with search terms reported in the PROSPERO protocol (S1 PROSPERO Protocol).

Only studies published in English were included in the systematic review and meta-analysis, although a sensitivity search identified no other relevant manuscripts published in other languages. The analysis focused exclusively on longitudinal observational studies evaluating the risk of NAION associated with semaglutide use in patients aged 12 years or older with type 2 diabetes, including prospective, retrospective, and registry-based studies.

Exclusion criteria for the systematic review and meta-analysis included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), other study designs, nonpeer-reviewed publications, and studies without clear documentation of semaglutide exposure or NAION-specific outcomes. For registry-based studies, the largest, most comprehensive cohort was retained to avoid double-counting overlapping populations, with equivalent population studies used as a sensitivity analysis as detailed in S5 Table.
The meta-analysis was synthesized using Cochrane's Review Manager (RevMan, v9.5.1) and R (v.4.5.1) with the metafor package (v.4.8).
The code for reproducibility is available in Zenodo at the DOI https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17885011.
The primary analysis used an inverse-variance fixed-effects model with Wald confidence intervals, while sensitivity analyses used the Hartung-Knapp random-effects method.
Heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran's Q test and reported as I-squared with a 95% confidence interval and p-value.

Sensitivity analyses included alternative synthesis scenarios using unadjusted hazard ratios, other NAION definition criteria, and consideration of replacement studies from overlapping source populations.
Small study effects and reporting bias were assessed using leave-one-out sensitivity testing.
The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE framework as implemented in GRADEpro GDT.
Comparator groups were defined as hierarchical treatment groupings: (A) treatment other than semaglutide, (B) other than GLP-1 RAs, and (C) specifically SGLT2i treatment.
The outcome definition for NAION was primarily based on International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10) diagnostic codes, with some studies verifying NAION against source medical documentation.

Studies identified semaglutide treatment using national prescription registries, though the studies by Cai and colleagues and Hathaway and colleagues did not provide detailed information on the definitions of semaglutide use.
To minimize dependence, at most one effect size per study was included within each comparator stratum, with residual dependence acknowledged as a limitation.
In cases with multiple NAION episodes, only the time to the first event was included in subsequent analyses.
No missing data handling or data-conversion methods were applied to the extracted data.
Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) and Risk of Bias in Non-Randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I, version 2).

The meta-analysis included 5 studies and 7 sensitivity analysis studies, with key characteristics detailed in S1 Table and exclusion details in S3 and S4 Tables. The majority of included studies were registry-based and enrolled patients aged >18 years, with two studies including patients aged ≥12 years and one sensitivity analysis study including only adults >65 years.

The meta-analysis was performed in three settings: A (semaglutide versus any other antidiabetic treatment, 386,207 versus 626,406 patients), B (semaglutide versus non-GLP-1 RAs, 279,753 versus 357,458 patients), and C (semaglutide versus SGLT2i, 104,997 versus 162,269 patients). A more precise definition of the comparator groups was unavailable, and patients in those groups might have been treated with a combination of diabetes treatments.

The study by Cai, 2025 [19] is a registry study of >18-year-old patients with type 2 diabetes comparing semaglutide (N=43,620) against dulaglutide (N=14,923), glipizide (N=44,092), sitagliptin (N=19,581), and empagliflozin (N=43,302), defining NAION via ICD10 codes occurring twice within 90 days over a ~2-year follow-up.

The study by Hsu, 2025 [16] is a registry study of ≥12-year-old patients with type 2 diabetes comparing semaglutide (N=174,584) against non-GLP-1 RAs (N=174,584), defining NAION via ICD10 codes over a ~5-year follow-up.

The study by Simonsen, 2025 [18] is a registry study of >18-year-old patients with type 2 diabetes comparing semaglutide (N=44,517 in Denmark, 16,860 in Norway) against SGLT2i (N=84,814 in Denmark, 34,153 in Norway), defining NAION via ICD10 codes H47.0 and H47.0c over a ~5-year follow-up.

The study by Grauslund, 2024 [17] is a registry study of >18-year-old patients with type 2 diabetes comparing semaglutide (N=106,454) against any other treatment (N=317,698), defining NAION via ICD10 code H47.0c over a ~5-year follow-up.

The study by Hathaway, 2024 [15] is a case-control study of ≥12-year-old patients with type 2 diabetes admitted to a neuroophthalmology clinic, comparing semaglutide (N=169) against non-GLP-1 RAs (N=234), defining NAION via ICD10 code H47.01 plus manual reviews in source documents over a ~3-year follow-up.
The meta-analysis utilized a Hartung-Knapp random-effects model, reporting an I² of 0% (95% CI: [0%, 92%]; p=0.538) for statistical heterogeneity across the five included studies.
All five included studies scored 6–7 out of 9 on the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) and were rated at moderate to serious risk of bias on the ROBINS-I v. 2 scale.

The meta-analysis included five observational studies (Cai 2025, Grauslund 2024, Hathaway 2024, Hsu 2025, Simonsen 2025) with total sample sizes ranging from 104,997 to 386,207 for the semaglutide vs. others comparison, and all studies scored 6-7 out of 9 on the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale.

The pooled hazard ratio for semaglutide versus non-GLP1 RA was 2.17 (95% CI 1.73-2.74) with low heterogeneity (I²=0%, Chi²=4.29, df=5, p=0.509), and the pooled hazard ratio for semaglutide versus SGLT2i was 1.96 (95% CI 1.28-2.99) with low heterogeneity (I²=0%, Chi²=3.94, df=5, p=0.558).

Replication is blocked by the fact that NAION diagnoses in the included studies were based on administrative coding without ophthalmologic confirmation, and key risk modifiers such as optic disc anatomy and rate of glycemic reduction were not accounted for.

The umbrella review identified 18 eligible publications, specifically 2 meta-analyses of RCTs (references 52, 53), 4 meta-analyses of observational studies (references 75-78), 9 systematic or structured narrative reviews (references 43-46, 48-51), and 2 statements (references 54, 55), along with 4 regulatory and safety communications from the EMA and WHO (references 56-60).

The two RCT meta-analyses reported odds ratios of 1.53 (95% CI [0.53, 4.44]; p=0.43) for GLP-1 RAs and 3.92 (95% CI [1.02, 15.03]; p=0.045) for semaglutide, noting that RCT data are underpowered to exclude a moderate increase in relative risk for the rare event of NAION.

Observational meta-analyses reported pooled adjusted hazard ratios ranging from 1.35 (95% CI [1.20, 1.52]; p<0.001) to 2.62 (95% CI [1.81, 3.80]; p<0.001) compared with non-GLP-1 regimens, with one study showing a nonsignificant odds ratio of 1.40 (95% CI [0.97, 2.04]; p=0.07).

The AMSTAR-2 assessment of the included meta-analyses yielded a confidence score of low to critically low due to the absence of a complete list of excluded items, the lack of a publication bias assessment, and the omission of key methodological details.

The systematic reviews received a critically low AMSTAR-2 confidence score due to the absence of complete lists of excluded items, the lack of publication bias assessments, and the omission of key methodological details.

The systematic reviews received a critically low AMSTAR-2 confidence score largely due to a general lack of registered protocols, excluded-study lists, study-level bias assessments, and key method details.

The meta-analysis of longitudinal observational studies reports that semaglutide use in patients with type 2 diabetes is associated with a hazard ratio for NAION ranging from 1.96 to 2.17 across comparator strata, with sensitivity analysis hazard ratios ranging from 1.26 to 4.95.

The analysis identified an absolute risk difference of 0.014% per year (95% CI [0.005%, 0.023%]) for NAION, which corresponds to approximately 1 additional NAION case per 7,000 patients treated for 1 year.
The study notes a potential for overdiagnosis of 40%-50% for NAION cases, which may reduce the true burden of the condition below the estimated 500 excess diagnostic codes per year.

Post-marketing reports from WHO VigiBase and FDA FAERS show a disproportionality signal for semaglutide and NAION with odds ratios ranging from 11.12 (95% CI [8.15, 15.16]) to 68.58 (95% CI [16.75, 280.67]), but these systems lack denominators and are subject to confounding by indication and channeling bias.

Pharmacovigilance time-trend analyses demonstrated an increase in NAION reports during 2023-2025, potentially driven by regulatory focus on diabetic retinopathy and guideline recommendations for closer ophthalmic surveillance in high-risk patients or after treatment intensification.

In a large Polish private care network including over 36,000 GLP-1 RA users and matched controls with up to 2 years' follow-up, GLP-1 RAs exposure was not an independent predictor of blindness, NAION, papilledema, or optic neuritis after multivariable adjustment, despite semaglutide being the most commonly used agent.

No current analysis considered glucose-lowering dynamics or fully adjusted for bias by indication, and semaglutide's potent glucose-lowering or blood pressure effects, particularly when combined with antihypertensive or diuretic therapies, may compromise optic nerve perfusion.
S1 Table provides details on the primary included studies, specifically their design, PICO framework, and follow-up period.
S2 Table contains further details on the primary included studies, including the definition and route of semaglutide use, assessed confounding factors, and the adjustment method.

S3 Table lists the characteristics of additional cohort studies, such as design, population, exposures, comparators, outcomes, and follow-up, along with reasons for their exclusion from the primary analysis.

The supplementary materials include S11 Table, which provides domain-level risk of bias and overall quality scores using the ROBINS-I and NOS tools for the observational studies included in the analysis.
S5 Table details the inter-study correlation assessment through the source dataset and identifies studies marked with an asterisk for the potential overlap-sensitivity analysis.
The systematic review reporting adheres to the PRISMA 2020 statement, with all 27 items addressed and their locations specified in the manuscript, as documented in S1 PRISMA Checklist.
The study protocol is registered in PROSPERO, with the registration form provided in S1 PROSPERO.

The meta-analysis relies on retrospective, mostly registry-based observational studies that reported hazard ratios, with only Cai and colleagues and Hathaway and colleagues utilizing specific diagnostic criteria for non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION).

The absence of a dedicated diagnostic code for non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) forced most source studies to rely on administrative coding, which may not accurately distinguish true NAION cases and introduces outcome misclassification risk.

The source studies lacked detailed clinical data on key risk modifiers such as optic disc anatomy and glycemic reduction rates, limiting the ability to adjust for confounding factors in the hazard ratio estimates.

The broad age range of patients included in the source studies, ranging from 12 years old to over 18, dilutes the true hazard ratio for semaglutide in the older population who are the primary recipients of the therapy and at higher risk for non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION).

Treatment duration and doses were not comprehensively reported in the source studies, and residual covariance of unrecorded factors such as frequency of ophthalmological consultations, smoking status, or history of cardiovascular disease may have persisted despite statistical adjustment.

Biases arising from potentially overlapping populations could not be resolved due to the inclusion of smaller national registries in multinational databases and the complexity of type 2 diabetes treatment regimens.

The results of the current meta-analysis are in opposition to those published by Özbek and colleagues, with the discrepancy suspected to arise from differences in the design and use of published adjusted models hazard ratios rather than recalculating hazard ratios to odds ratios.

The current meta-analysis results align with Goldenberg and colleagues (hazard ratio of 1.60, 95% confidence interval [1.12, 2.31]; p=0.01) and Ho and colleagues (hazard ratio of 1.35, 95% confidence interval [1.20, 1.52]; p<0.001).
The Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) is the specified tool for assessing the quality of nonrandomised studies in the meta-analysis.
The ROBINS-I tool is the specified method for assessing risk of bias in non-randomized studies of interventions.
The PRISMA 2020 statement is the required guideline for reporting the systematic review.
The Methodological Expectations of Cochrane Intervention Reviews (MECIR) standards define the conduct and reporting requirements for the review.
The GRADE Handbook is the specified tool for assessing the certainty of evidence.
The AMSTAR 2 tool is the specified instrument for critical appraisal of the systematic reviews included in the analysis.
The European Medicines Agency PRAC concluded that non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) is a very rare side effect of the semaglutide medicines Ozempic, Rybelsus, and Wegovy.
The FDA adverse event reporting system was the data source used for the disproportionality analysis regarding semaglutide and nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy.
The SELECT trial was the source data for the modelling study on the population-level impact of semaglutide 2.4 mg.

The meta-analysis relies on administrative coding rather than specific diagnostic criteria for NAION, creating a data gap where the exact diagnostic definitions used in the source studies are not specified, which blocks replication of the misclassification bias assessment.

The power analysis supports only a specific subgroup rather than the broad population claim, and the exact sample size and reported effect size with its 95% confidence interval are not provided, which are necessary parameters to determine if the general conclusion is statistically underpowered.

The study's methods section fails to specify whether ICD-10 codes were validated against clinical charts, creating a critical gap in the data acquisition pipeline that blocks independent replication of the diagnostic coding process.

Replication is blocked by the absence of data on unmeasured confounders such as baseline cardiovascular health and smoking status, which are missing from the registries and prevent distinguishing a true association from coding error or confounding.
The study used the TriNetX US Collaborative Network of electronic health records from 2010 to 2024, including adults aged 40-69 years with type 2 diabetes and at least 1 year of follow-up.

The study classified patients into five treatment groups: metformin only (reference), metformin plus DPP-4 inhibitors, metformin plus GLP-1 receptor agonists, metformin plus SGLT-2 inhibitors, and insulin monotherapy.
Exposure was defined by the first recorded prescription and continued use during the follow-up period.
Propensity score matching was applied to balance covariates in the retrospective cohort study.
All relevant data for the study are available within the paper and its Supporting Information files.
The study population comprised 1,528,885 adults with type 2 diabetes, with a mean age of 58 years and 49.2% women.

Exposure was defined by the first recorded prescription and continued use during follow-up for four antidiabetic medication groups: metformin plus GLP-1 receptor agonists, metformin plus SGLT-2 inhibitors, and insulin monotherapy.
Primary outcomes of incident mild cognitive disorder, Alzheimer disease, and vascular dementia were identified using ICD-10 codes.
Hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals were estimated from Cox proportional hazards models, utilizing landmark analyses for follow-up periods shorter and longer than 5 years.

GLP-1 receptor agonists plus metformin were associated with hazard ratios of 0.46 (95% CI, 0.37-0.57) for vascular dementia, 0.79 (95% CI, 0.66-0.95) for mild cognitive disorder, and 0.46 (95% CI, 0.31-0.70) for Alzheimer disease.
SGLT-2 inhibitors plus metformin were associated with a hazard ratio of 0.68 (95% CI, 0.54-0.87) for vascular dementia, with no significant association reported for other outcomes.

Insulin monotherapy was associated with hazard ratios of 3.27 (95% CI, 3.03-3.52) for vascular dementia, 1.71 (95% CI, 1.56-1.87) for mild cognitive disorder, and 1.56 (95% CI, 1.32-1.84) for Alzheimer disease.

The standard Cox models used in the analysis do not account for death as a competing event, meaning reported hazard ratios reflect cause-specific hazards rather than cumulative incidence, particularly for the insulin group where mortality and censoring were higher.

The study used the TriNetX US Collaborative Network, which contains deidentified electronic health records from more than 118 million patients across 69 health care organizations, with data coded using ICD-9 and ICD-10. Analyses were conducted within the TriNetX platform using its built-in analytic tools for cohort creation and outcome comparisons.

Eligible participants were adults aged 40-69 years with a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus who had at least 1 year of follow-up after the index date, defined as the first prescription of an antidiabetic medication. Exclusion criteria included Type 1 diabetes mellitus (ICD10 CM:E10), Human immunodeficiency virus disease (ICD10 CM:B20), pre-existing diagnoses of dementia or cognitive impairment, and incomplete demographic or clinical data.

Patients were classified into 5 mutually exclusive treatment groups based on their first recorded antidiabetic regimen: metformin only, metformin plus dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors, metformin plus glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists, metformin plus sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors, and insulin monotherapy. The primary outcomes were incident diagnoses of mild cognitive disorder (ICD-10 G31.84), Alzheimer disease (ICD-10 G30), and vascular dementia (ICD-10 F01), assessed beginning 1 day after the index date.

Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed using a greedy nearest-neighbor algorithm with a caliper width of 0.1 pooled standard deviations, including covariates for age, sex, race, ethnicity, sleep apnea, hypothyroidism, tobacco use, alcohol use, head injury, glucocorticoid use, and glycated hemoglobin.

Cardiovascular disease and renal disease were excluded from propensity score covariates due to the complexity of capturing these heterogeneously coded conditions within the TriNetX platform, which is acknowledged as a study limitation.

Hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals were estimated using Cox proportional hazards models, with proportionality evaluated using scaled Schoenfeld residuals and landmark analyses conducted at less than 5 years and 5 years or longer.
The Benjamini-Hochberg method was applied to control the false discovery rate, and two-sided P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

The study utilized deidentified patient data from the TriNetX platform in compliance with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, and the Saint Louis University Institutional Review Board determined the study was exempt from review because only aggregate, deidentified data were used.

Table 1 provides mean and median follow-up duration in days for each treatment group (Metformin + DPP-4i, Metformin Only, Metformin + GLP-1 RA, Metformin + SGLT-2i, Insulin Monotherapy) stratified by landmark periods of less than 5 years and 5 years or longer after propensity score matching.
The study screened 51,859,560 patient records to identify 1,528,885 eligible adults aged 40-69 years with type 2 diabetes, with a mean age of 58 years and 49.2% women.

Pre-matching treatment group sizes were 446,109 for metformin only, 43,519 for metformin plus DPP-4 inhibitors, 115,362 for metformin plus GLP-1 receptor agonists, 59,691 for metformin plus SGLT-2 inhibitors, and 368,668 for insulin monotherapy.

After 1:1 propensity score matching, comparator cohort sizes were 43,383 for DPP-4 inhibitors (0.3% unmatched), 102,399 for GLP-1 receptor agonists (11.2% unmatched), 58,327 for SGLT-2 inhibitors (2.3% unmatched), and 333,153 for insulin (9.6% unmatched).

Residual hemoglobin A1c imbalances after matching had standardized mean differences of 0.164 for the DPP-4 inhibitor group, 0.152 for the SGLT-2 inhibitor group, 0.079 for the insulin group, and 0.021 for the GLP-1 receptor agonist group.
The landmark period of less than 5 years includes outcomes occurring 1-1,825 days after the index date, while the landmark period of 5 years or longer includes outcomes occurring after 1,825 days.
Insulin monotherapy users had a median follow-up of 303 days compared to 612 days for matched metformin-only users across both landmark periods.

The study used the TriNetX Network Platform to create unmatched original cohorts and 1:1 matched groups, with the specific procedures documented in Fig 1 (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0356138.g001).

The analysis utilized Cox proportional hazards models for all estimates, with each combination group matched 1:1 to a metformin-only comparator and landmark analysis performed at <5 years and ≥5 years of follow-up.
Unadjusted pre-matching outcome comparisons are available in Supplementary S5 Table, which is required for full replication of the baseline data.

Figure 2 presents propensity score-matched hazard ratios for vascular dementia, mild cognitive disorder, and Alzheimer disease, comparing metformin plus DPP-4 inhibitors, metformin plus GLP-1 receptor agonists, metformin plus SGLT-2 inhibitors, and insulin monotherapy against metformin alone, stratified by follow-up duration of less than 5 years versus 2 years.

Table 3 reports cognitive outcomes for patients receiving metformin plus SGLT-2 inhibitors (N=58,327 matched pairs) or insulin monotherapy (N=333,153 matched pairs) compared with metformin only, after propensity score matching, with specific case counts, hazard ratios, 95% confidence intervals, and p-values for vascular dementia, mild cognitive disorder, and Alzheimer disease across follow-up periods of less than 5 years and 5 years or more.
The study is available at https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0356138.t004.
DPP-4 inhibitors increase endogenous GLP-1 and GIP levels, but the magnitude of GLP-1 elevation achieved with DPP-4 inhibitors is substantially lower than that achieved with GLP-1 receptor agonists.

The study used propensity score matching with administrative data to balance differences in disease severity, though residual confounding by indication remains a potential limitation for insulin monotherapy findings.

The study used Cox proportional hazards models for all estimates and matched each treatment group 1:1 to a metformin-only comparator. Insulin monotherapy was used without metformin, and the landmark analysis was conducted at <5 years and ≥5 years of follow-up.
Unadjusted pre-matching outcome comparisons are available in Supplementary S6 Table. The data and code availability is indicated by the DOI https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0356138.t003.

Table 4 reports Absolute Risk Differences (ARD) per 1,000 Person-Years after propensity score matching for outcomes including Vascular Dementia, Mild Cognitive Disorder, and Alzheimer Disease across time windows of <5 years and ≥5 years. The ARD was calculated as the incidence rate of the comparator group minus the incidence rate of the metformin-only group.
The Absolute Risk Difference (ARD) calculation used the mean follow-up duration from Table 1. The data and code availability is indicated by the DOI https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0356138.t004.

Formal competing risk analyses were not performed in the study, which is a methodological limitation requiring that the reported hazard ratios be interpreted as cause-specific hazards rather than estimates of cumulative incidence.

The median follow-up duration for the insulin group was 303 days, which is a two-fold difference compared to the 612 days in the matched metformin group, indicating that insulin users were censored earlier likely due to death or loss to follow-up.

The supporting information includes S1 through S4 tables detailing baseline characteristics for four specific treatment comparisons: Metformin and DPP-4 inhibitors (Group 2) vs Metformin only (Group 1), Metformin and GLP-1 receptor agonists (Group 3) vs Metformin only (Group 1), Metformin and SGLT-2 inhibitors (Group 4) vs Metformin only (Group 1), and Insulin only (Group 5) vs Metformin only (Group 1).

Supporting information S5 and S6 tables present cognitive outcomes for patients receiving metformin plus DPP-4 inhibitors and metformin plus SGLT-2 inhibitors, respectively, compared with metformin only, specifically for unmatched cohorts prior to propensity score matching with a comparator group size of N=446,109.
The supporting information files S1 through S6 are provided in DOCX format.
Ahmad Basil Nasir is credited with data curation and formal analysis for the study.

The study matched metformin-only users across landmark periods of 303 days and 612 days, noting that higher censoring rates were attributable to advanced disease severity and competing mortality risk.
In matched analyses, the group receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists plus metformin (n=102,399) was compared against the metformin-alone group (n=102,399) to assess outcomes.
For the GLP-1 receptor agonists plus metformin group, the incidence of vascular dementia was 124 cases versus 243 cases in the metformin-alone group, with a hazard ratio of 0.46 (95% CI, 0.37-0.57).

For the GLP-1 receptor agonists plus metformin group, the incidence of mild cognitive disorder was 216 cases versus 242 cases in the metformin-alone group, with a hazard ratio of 0.79 (95% CI, 0.66-0.95).
For the GLP-1 receptor agonists plus metformin group, the incidence of Alzheimer disease was 34 cases versus 66 cases in the metformin-alone group, with a hazard ratio of 0.46 (95% CI, 0.31-0.70).

The absolute risk difference for vascular dementia in the GLP-1 receptor agonists plus metformin group was -0.93 per 1,000 person-years at less than 5 years and -0.88 per 1,000 person-years at 5 years or longer.

In the SGLT-2 inhibitors plus metformin group (n=58,327), the incidence of vascular dementia at less than 5 years was 114 cases versus 157 cases in the comparison group, with a hazard ratio of 0.68 (95% CI, 0.54-0.87).
The DPP-4 inhibitors plus metformin group (n=43,383) showed no significant association with vascular dementia, mild cognitive disorder, or Alzheimer disease at either follow-up interval.

The insulin monotherapy group (n=333,153) had a vascular dementia incidence of 2,630 cases versus 966 cases in matched metformin-only patients at less than 5 years, with a hazard ratio of 3.27 (95% CI, 3.03-3.52).

The insulin monotherapy group (n=333,153) had a mild cognitive disorder incidence of 1,088 cases versus 781 cases in matched metformin-only patients at less than 5 years, with a hazard ratio of 1.71 (95% CI, 1.56-1.87).

The insulin monotherapy group (n=333,153) had an Alzheimer disease incidence of 327 cases versus 254 cases in matched metformin-only patients at less than 5 years, with a hazard ratio of 1.56 (95% CI, 1.32-1.84).
The study population was restricted to adults aged 40-69 years, which limits the generalizability of the findings to older adults.
Residual hemoglobin A1c imbalance after propensity score matching was 0.164 for DPP-4 inhibitors and 0.152 for SGLT-2 inhibitors, both exceeding the 0.1 threshold.

The propensity score matching excluded cardiovascular disease severity, renal function, diabetes duration, APOE ε4 genotype, education level, physical activity, and socioeconomic status from the model.

All combination therapy groups in the study included metformin as a backbone agent, which may attenuate the apparent cognitive benefits of add-on agents through vitamin B12 depletion and hyperhomocysteinemia.
The observational design relied on ICD-10 codes for diagnoses, which may be subject to misclassification and underdetection of early or mild cognitive disease.
The study data was sourced from TriNetX, which captures data from diverse US health systems.
The absence of a competing risk framework means that differential mortality across groups, particularly for insulin users, may have influenced outcome ascertainment.

The Hartung-Knapp random-effects model parameters are not fully specified for replication, as only the I² statistic (0% with a 95% CI of [0%, 92%]) and pooled odds ratio range (11.12 to 68.58) are reported, without the underlying effect sizes or variances from the five included studies.

The analysis lacks sensitivity analyses accounting for unmeasured confounders such as smoking or cardiovascular history, which are not captured in the available registry data, creating an unquantified gap in the causal inference pipeline.

The outcome definition appears to capture broader optic nerve ischemia rather than specific NAION, a mislabeling that renders the pooled hazard ratio uninterpretable for the intended clinical endpoint and prevents integration with prior semaglutide studies.
All data generated and analyzed in the cost-effectiveness study of semaglutide versus dulaglutide are provided within the manuscript.
The Markov model simulating type 2 diabetes mellitus disease progression uses a 25-year time horizon.
Transition probabilities between health states in the Markov model are sourced from the UK Prospective Diabetes Study Outcomes Model (UKPDS 82) and the SUSTAIN 7 clinical trial.
Health utility values for the Markov model are obtained from published literature using the Chinese EQ-5D-5L value set.

The cost-effectiveness analysis projected 25-year outcomes using cohort simulation, with a total cost of ¥193,353.07 and 11.628 quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) for dulaglutide, and a total cost of ¥240,925.08 and 11.900 QALYs for semaglutide.
The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) for semaglutide compared with dulaglutide was ¥174,904 per QALY gained, which is approximately twice China's 2023 per capita GDP of ¥89,358.
The study applied the Chinese Guidelines for Pharmacoeconomic Evaluation (2020), which defines the economically acceptable range as an ICER between 1 and 3 times the per capita GDP.

Probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) determined that at a willingness-to-pay threshold of 3 times the per capita GDP (¥268,074), semaglutide had an 89.6% probability of being considered economically acceptable.
The study received funding under grant number 2022QH1124, with Chen Qiying as the recipient, and the funder had no role in the study design, data collection, analysis, or publication decisions.

The study developed a Markov state-transition model integrating international clinical trial data with contemporary Chinese parameters to evaluate the lifetime cost-effectiveness of semaglutide versus dulaglutide in managing Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus. The study adhered to the Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Reporting Standards 2022 (CHEERS 2022) for design and reporting, with details provided in S1 Table.

The study's Markov model for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) consists of three states: "diabetes without complications," "diabetes with complications," and "death." The model uses transition probabilities P1 (remain uncomplicated), P2 (progress to complications), P3 (death from uncomplicated), P4 (remain complicated), and P5 (death from complications), with death as an absorbing state and no reverse transition from complicated to uncomplicated states.
The study adhered to the Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Reporting Standards 2022 (CHEERS 2022) for design and reporting, with details provided in S1 Table.

The disease state transition probabilities and health utility values for the aggregated 'diabetes with complications' state were derived as a prevalence-weighted average of the probabilities for major complication subtypes. The specific calculation formula for this weighting strategy is detailed in a subsequent section of the document.

The weights for the composite calculation of complications were based on the real-world prevalence profile of macrovascular (68%), microvascular (19%), and co-existing complications (13%) as reported by the China National Diabetes and Metabolic Disorders Study (CNDMDS) 2023 [17]. The source data for these weights is cross-sectional prevalence data from the CNDMDS 2023 study.

The Markov model used 1-year cycle lengths, a starting cohort age of 50 years, and a 25-year time horizon ending at age 75. A 5% annual discount rate was applied to both costs and health outcomes, with sensitivity analyses testing discount rates between 0% and 8%.

The model was constructed using TreeAge Pro (TreeAge Software, Williamstown, MA) and involved sequential analyses including rollback computation, Markov cohort simulation, Monte Carlo simulation, and sensitivity analysis.

Semaglutide was priced at ¥813.96 per 4 mg pen (maintenance dose 1 mg/week) and dulaglutide at ¥123.55 per 1.5 mg vial (maintenance dose 1.5 mg/week), both using 2023 National Reimbursement Drug List prices. Routine management costs were set at ¥3,860/year and complication treatment costs at ¥19,720/year, both derived from the CNDMDS 2023 national Diagnosis-Related Group (DRG) database.

The utility value for the diabetes without complications health state was set to 0.88, derived from the Chinese EQ-5D-5L value set applied to a cross-sectional survey of urban Chinese adults (N ≈ 1,296) and age-weighted to the 30-59-year stratum.

The study utilized glycemic outcome data, specifically changes in HbA1c, systolic blood pressure, and body weight over a 40-week treatment period, extracted from the SUSTAIN 7 trial (reference [22]), a multinational, randomized, open-label, phase 3b study comparing once-weekly semaglutide versus dulaglutide in adults with type 2 diabetes and baseline HbA1c levels of 7.0% to 10.5%.

Incidence rates for diabetes-related complications were obtained from the UKPDS82 study (reference [29]), and transition parameters for the Markov model were generated by integrating HbA1c changes from the SUSTAIN 7 trial with complication probabilities from UKPDS82.

The relative treatment effect of semaglutide versus dulaglutide was estimated by applying HbA1c, systolic blood pressure, and body weight reduction differences to the established risk equations from UKPDS82 (reference [29]) to derive annual transition probabilities between health states in the Markov model.

For microvascular complications, the risk reduction was estimated at approximately 37% (range: 33%-41%), with a 10% relative reduction in HbA1c corresponding to a risk reduction of approximately 35%-41%, modeled using a Beta distribution to reflect uncertainty bounded between 0 and 1.

For macrovascular complications, a conservative uniform distribution was used to represent the potential range of risk reduction due to the lack of statistical significance for early intensive glucose-lowering benefits.
Annual transition probabilities were derived from event rates using the declining exponential approximation of life expectancy (DEALE) formula (reference [30]).

The baseline health utility for the no-complications state was 0.88, derived from the Chinese EQ-5D-5L value set and age-weighted to the 30-59-year stratum. The utility for the death state was defined as 0.00.

Health utility values for type 2 diabetes complication states were obtained from a cross-sectional study of 2,202 Chinese community-dwelling adults with type 2 diabetes conducted by Huang et al. [28].

The weighted average utility for the composite "diabetes with complications" state was calculated as 0.74 using the formula (0.68 × 0.735) + (0.19 × 0.791) + (0.13 × 0.701), based on complication profiles from the CNDMDS 2023 (macrovascular: 68%; microvascular: 19%; co-existing: 13%).

The drug cost for Semaglutide was ¥10,548.92 and for Dulaglutide was ¥6,242.60 in the complication-free state, with a background treatment cost of ¥3,860.00 for both. In the with-complications state, the drug cost for Semaglutide remained ¥10,548.92 while Dulaglutide increased to ¥6,424.60, with a complication treatment cost of ¥19,720.00 for both drugs.

The total cost for Semaglutide was ¥14,408.92 in the complication-free state and ¥34,128.92 in the with-complications state. The total cost for Dulaglutide was ¥10,284.60 in the complication-free state and ¥30,004.60 in the with-complications state.

The health utility value for macrovascular events was 0.735 ± 0.108, for microvascular events was 0.791 ± 0.101, and for both macrovascular and microvascular events was 0.701 ± 0.115, as referenced in citations [25,28].
Annual transition probabilities were derived from event rates using the declining exponential approximation of life expectancy (DEALE) formula: P = 1 - exp(-rt).

The modeling strategy leverages the UKPDS82 dataset to incorporate combined effects of risk factors including systolic blood pressure, lipid profiles, body weight, smoking status, and renal function, rather than attributing complication risks solely to HbA1c changes.
The willingness-to-pay threshold was set at three times China's 2023 per-capita GDP of ¥89,358, resulting in a threshold value of ¥268,074 to ensure temporal consistency with 2023 cost inputs.
Sensitivity analyses included one-way variation of critical parameters and probabilistic sensitivity analysis using beta distributions for probabilities and gamma distributions for costs.
The Markov cohort model was developed in TreeAge Pro software, and half-cycle corrections were applied to costs, health utilities, and other relevant parameters.

The Monte Carlo simulation used 1,000 iterations with Beta distributions for health utility values and Normal distributions for the discount rate, where standard deviations were derived using the formula (Upper limit - Lower limit) / (2 × 1.96).
The baseline willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold was set at ¥268,074 per QALY for the cost-effectiveness analysis of semaglutide versus dulaglutide.
Full distributional specifications for the model parameters are detailed in Table 5 of the document.

The one-way sensitivity analysis varied costs between health states, health-state utilities, the discount rate, and the unit price of semaglutide, with specific adjustments including a 25% cost reduction for both semaglutide and dulaglutide strategies and a further 20% reduction for the semaglutide unit price.

The semaglutide unit price baseline is ¥813.96 per pen, reduced from an initial launch price of ¥1,904.00, while health-state utilities were varied by ±10% and the discount rate was tested across a range of 0% to 8%.

The cost-effectiveness analysis results for the 25-year time horizon show a total cost of ¥193,353.07 and 11.628 QALYs for Dulaglutide, and a total cost of ¥240,925.08 and 11.900 QALYs for Semaglutide, yielding an ICER of ¥174,904/QALY.
The probabilistic sensitivity analysis assigned Gamma distributions to cost parameters to assess the robustness of the cost-effectiveness findings.

The model input parameters include Semaglutide cost (complication-free) with a Gamma distribution (mean 14470.55, standard deviation 922.87), Semaglutide cost (with complications) with a Gamma distribution (mean 34190.55, standard deviation 2180.52), and Semaglutide unit price with a Gamma distribution (mean 813.96, standard deviation 41.53).

The model input parameters include Dulaglutide cost (complication-free) with a Gamma distribution (mean 10291.82, standard deviation 656.37) and Dulaglutide cost (with complications) with a Gamma distribution (mean 30011.82, standard deviation 1914.02).

The model input parameters include Health utility value (complication-free) with a Beta distribution (mean 0.88, standard deviation 0.05), Health utility value (with complications) with a Beta distribution (mean 0.74, standard deviation 0.04), and Discount rate with a Normal distribution (mean 0.05, standard deviation 0.02).

The study employed a Markov model using discrete-time simulation to extrapolate short-term clinical indicators to a lifetime horizon, specifically to address the 40-week duration limitation of the SUSTAIN-7 trial.
The model was built using TreeAge Pro software, and half-cycle corrections were applied to costs, health utilities, and other relevant parameters.
The transition probability from the Complication-Free Diabetes State to the With complications state (P2) is 0.0273 for Metformin, 0.0235 for Dulaglutide, and 0.0172 for Semaglutide.
The transition probability from the Complication-Free Diabetes State to the Death State (P3) is 0.0068 for Metformin, 0.0058 for Dulaglutide, and 0.0042 for Semaglutide.
The transition probability from the Diabetes-Related Complications State to the Death State (P5) is 0.0067 for Metformin, 0.0057 for Dulaglutide, and 0.0042 for Semaglutide.
A 35-year scenario analysis was incorporated to simulate patients up to age 85 years to evaluate the impact of an extended time horizon on the ICER.
Over a 25-year time horizon, Semaglutide had total costs of ¥240,925.08 and 11.900 QALYs compared to Dulaglutide's ¥193,353.07 and 11.628 QALYs, resulting in an ICER of ¥174,904 per QALY gained.
Over a 35-year time horizon, Semaglutide yielded an ICER of ¥142,481 per QALY, with incremental costs of ¥53,897.41 and incremental QALYs of 0.378.
The willingness-to-pay threshold used for comparison was China's 2023 3x GDP per capita, calculated as ¥268,074 per QALY.
At cycle 25 of the Markov cohort simulation, the proportion of patients in the death state was 9.99% for Semaglutide and 13.80% for Dulaglutide.
At cycle 25 of the Markov cohort simulation, the proportion of patients in the complication-free state was 58.23% for Semaglutide and 47.54% for Dulaglutide.

The model utilizes a conventional Markov structure with static transition probabilities over a 25-year horizon, applying half-cycle corrections to costs and health utilities but failing to capture dynamic risk evolution or time-varying complication risks.

Most model parameters, including drug costs and health utility values, were obtained from Chinese data sources, while disease transition probabilities primarily relied on epidemiological data from Western populations such as UKPDS.
The cost analysis was limited to direct medical costs, excluding indirect and intangible costs that constitute components of the total economic burden.

The model assumed continuous use of semaglutide or dulaglutide over the entire 25-year simulation period, ignoring real-world treatment discontinuation, switching, or escalation to basal insulin documented in Chinese real-world studies.

The model was based mainly on glycemic and macrovascular endpoints derived from the SUSTAIN-7 trial and did not explicitly incorporate the protective effect of semaglutide against atrial fibrillation due to a lack of direct head-to-head comparative data between semaglutide and dulaglutide.
The study utilized long-term Markov model simulations to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of semaglutide relative to dulaglutide for type 2 diabetes patients in China.
The calculated incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) for semaglutide was ¥174,904 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY).
The cost-effectiveness threshold used for the evaluation was defined as three times China's gross domestic product (GDP).
The study's generalizability is limited by the lack of real-world treatment patterns and Chinese-specific epidemiological data in the current analysis.
The study reports adherence to the Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Reporting Standards 2022 (CHEERS 2022) checklist for health economic evaluations.
The Markov model simulated a 25-year horizon, calculating total costs of ¥193,353.07 and 11.628 QALYs for the dulaglutide regimen, and ¥240,925.08 and 11.900 QALYs for the semaglutide regimen.
The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio for semaglutide compared to dulaglutide was ¥174,904 per QALY gained, with an incremental health gain of 0.272 QALYs.

The study utilized a long-term continuous treatment design that integrated glycemic, weight, and blood pressure reductions over a 25-year horizon to generate China-specific ICERs using local parameters.
The semaglutide ICER of ¥174,904/QALY was evaluated against China's three-times-GDP threshold to confirm cost-effectiveness.

The specific medical codes used to identify the ocular condition were not provided in the manuscript, creating a critical gap that prevents verification of whether the outcome was correctly classified or if it captured a broader group of eye issues.

The random-effects 95% confidence interval for the reported association has not been demonstrated to exclude the null value of 1.0, meaning the statistical evidence is insufficient to rule out chance and the point estimate of 68.58 is not reproducible as a significant finding.

The authors failed to provide exact definitions and tools to distinguish the specific outcome from other ocular conditions, which blocks replication by making it impossible to verify if the causal inference is based on the correct diagnosis or general optic neuropathy.

The supplementary materials containing the specific ICD-10 code lists required to verify the exclusion of diabetic or arteritic optic neuropathies are behind a public access fee, creating a procedural barrier that prevents immediate reproducibility audits of the coding phase.

The Simonsen 2025 registry subset explicitly defines NAION using ICD-10 codes H47.0 and H47.0c, but the systematic review component pools heterogeneous observational data without documenting how individual studies handled these specific exclusion codes, leaving a gap in the processing pipeline that cannot be audited from the report.

The meta-analytic aggregation is invalid for replication because the pooled estimate relies on unverified coding in the constituent studies, leaving half of the data foundation opaque and preventing the reconstruction of the risk estimate.

The cognitive benefit analysis depends on unblinded administrative codes that do not isolate the drug's impact from patient baseline health status, preventing replication of the claim that the medication provides neuroprotection rather than reflecting selection bias.

The NAION risk finding is statistically indeterminate due to a low certainty rating, preventing the integration of this safety signal with prior observational work and leaving the association unverified pending ophthalmologic confirmation.

The umbrella review aggregates heterogeneous studies using inconsistent clinical criteria rather than uniform adjudication, which blocks the replication of the NAION signal as a consistent biological effect and leaves the safety risk unconfirmed.

The manuscript lacks raw administrative codes and adjudication protocols necessary to verify the NAION signal, making the safety finding an unverified hypothesis that cannot be independently confirmed or refuted.

The cost-effectiveness model uses fixed parameters that ignore regional price variations and real-world adherence, meaning the economic superiority is only valid within those specific assumptions and cannot be replicated in different contexts without adjusting for these missing variables.

The uncorrected multiple-comparison issue strips the secondary cognitive endpoints of statistical validity, leaving only the primary outcome as a potentially robust finding and requiring a proper correction for family-wise error to validate the broader neuroprotective narrative.

To resolve the conflicting findings between the administrative data meta-analysis and the Polish cohort study, a new prospective study with sufficient statistical power to detect rare events and independent ophthalmologic adjudication is required, as retrospective analysis of noisy ICD-coded records is insufficient for replication.

documents: The association between semaglutide use and nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) is currently supported only by recent case reports, which provide insufficient evidence to establish a definitive causal link.

The evaluation of semaglutide's risk profile for nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) is limited to observational studies, which are subject to confounding variables and cannot rule out alternative explanations for the observed outcomes.

The meta-analysis relied on observational studies, which are inherently susceptible to confounding variables and residual bias that cannot be fully eliminated by the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale or ROBINS-I assessments.

The use of fixed-effects models for calculating pooled hazard ratios assumes that the true effect size is identical across all included studies, a condition that may not hold if there is significant heterogeneity in study populations or methodologies.

The search strategy was limited to specific databases and a defined time frame (January 2023 to November 2025), which may exclude relevant earlier literature or studies indexed in other repositories, potentially introducing selection bias into the synthesized evidence.

The association between semaglutide use and nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) is derived exclusively from retrospective, registry-based observational studies, meaning the findings are subject to study-level outcome misclassification and confounding that could invalidate the causal link.

Because the evidence synthesis relies solely on observational data rather than randomized controlled trials, the reported hazard ratios for semaglutide and NAION may not hold if unmeasured confounders or biases in the registry data are present.

The meta-analysis included studies relying on retrospective, registry-based designs and International Classification of Diseases codes to identify nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) cases, which introduces potential misclassification and confounding by indication.

Because the included studies were assessed as having a moderate to serious risk of bias and the overall certainty of evidence was graded as low to very low, the findings regarding the association between semaglutide and NAION should be interpreted with caution.

The pooled hazard ratio estimates from the meta-analysis are limited by the lack of standardized NAION diagnostic criteria in the underlying studies, necessitating high-quality, prospective studies to confirm the results and accurately identify individuals at the greatest risk.

The reported association between semaglutide therapy and NAION is based on registry-based cohort studies and pharmacovigilance reports rather than randomized controlled trials, which may limit the causal inference of the observed elevated risk.

The evidence synthesis for the association between semaglutide and NAION is limited by its exclusive reliance on retrospective, registry-based observational studies, which introduces potential biases from study-level outcome misclassification and confounding.

The low certainty of the available evidence regarding semaglutide and NAION risk means that the observed association may not hold under rigorous conditions, necessitating further high-quality studies to clarify the true relationship.

The exact association between semaglutide and NAION incidence remains not fully elucidated, and current registry and pharmacovigilance evidence requires synthesis with a specific focus on managing bias and confounding to determine validity.

The finding that semaglutide increases the hazard for NAION compared to other antidiabetic treatments is derived from longitudinal observational real-world studies, which may be subject to confounding factors not present in randomized controlled trials.

The discrepancy between observational meta-analyses showing increased NAION risk and randomized controlled trial meta-analyses reporting fewer NAION events suggests that the observed association in observational data may be driven by confounding rather than a direct causal effect of semaglutide.

The association between semaglutide and NAION is heavily confounded by indication because established NAION risk factors, such as older age, hypertension, and diabetes, are also the primary indications for semaglutide use, making it difficult to isolate the drug's specific effect from underlying disease severity.

Meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials failed to show a statistically significant increase in NAION risk for semaglutide, but this null finding is limited by extremely small event counts due to the low absolute risk of the condition and the potential under-representation of highest-risk patient populations in these trials.

The EMA's conclusion that semaglutide doubles the risk of NAION is based on observational data that may not fully account for the confounding by indication present in the source studies, where patients with higher baseline cardiovascular and metabolic risks are more likely to receive the treatment.

The assumption of continuous use of semaglutide or dulaglutide over the entire 25-year simulation period represents an idealized treatment pathway that ignores real-world discontinuation or switching, thereby potentially overestimating the long-term benefits of both agents.

The extrapolation of short-term clinical indicators to a lifetime horizon using discrete-time simulation relies on model assumptions that may not hold under real-world conditions, making the long-term endpoints like mortality and quality-adjusted life years dependent on the accuracy of these structural assumptions rather than direct empirical observation.

The cost-effectiveness conclusion for semaglutide relies on long-term Markov model simulations rather than observed data, meaning the findings may not hold if real-world treatment patterns or adherence differ from the model's assumptions.

The study explicitly acknowledges that its generalizability is limited because it lacks real-world treatment patterns and Chinese-specific epidemiological data, which are necessary to confirm the robustness of the pharmacoeconomic findings.

The cost-effectiveness of once-weekly semaglutide versus dulaglutide for type 2 diabetes in China relies on hypothetical modeling exercises rather than direct head-to-head clinical trial data, meaning the comparative efficacy and safety assumptions may not reflect real-world patient outcomes or adherence patterns.

The comparison of injection-site experience between semaglutide and dulaglutide is limited to a trial in healthy subjects, so the findings may not generalize to patients with type 2 diabetes who have different skin integrity, comorbidities, or injection histories.

The rapid review and meta-analysis of real-world studies on semaglutide for type 2 diabetes mellitus is subject to the inherent heterogeneity and potential biases of observational real-world data, which may introduce confounding variables not present in randomized controlled trials.

The statistical significance of the point estimate 68.58 for NAION risk is unreliable for validity assessment because the specific ICD-10 code lists required to rule out misclassification were not provided, making it impossible to calculate the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval.

The methodological coherence of the three papers is compromised because two rely on retrospective registry data with variable ICD-10 code definitions for NAION while the third uses prospective cohort methods, creating a heterogeneity in outcome definitions that prevents direct meta-analytic comparison without specified harmonization protocols.

The PLOS ONE cohort's reliance on unvalidated administrative data creates a critical ambiguity where 'continued use' may reflect pharmacy refill patterns rather than actual adherence, potentially biasing the denominator and invalidating the exposure classification necessary to support the cognitive benefit claims.

The umbrella review aggregates heterogeneous studies relying on inconsistent clinical criteria rather than uniform adjudication, which undermines the ability to treat the NAION signal as a consistent biological effect. Consequently, the safety data conflicts with prior RCTs and remains purely descriptive, meaning the risk may not exist as a consistent phenomenon but rather as an artifact of the lack of standardized diagnostic pipelines.

The practical replication blocker is the absence of raw patient-level data and the specific ICD codes used, which prevents verification of whether diagnostic criteria were applied consistently across the eighteen included studies. Without these elements, the NAION signal cannot be distinguished from inconsistencies in data recording practices, leaving the validity of the safety concern unproven.

The conclusion that the primary cognitive outcome is statistically robust while secondary endpoints are invalid due to multiple-comparison issues overlooks the potential for confounding by indication, where the primary effect might be driven by unmeasured baseline differences rather than a direct drug mechanism, especially since the study design does not fully account for family-wise error in the context of the broader neuroprotective narrative.

The advice to maintain regular eye exams as the best protection against unconfirmed NAION risk assumes that the current monitoring protocol is adequate to detect the specific vascular event in question, which may not be true if the condition presents with subtle signs that standard exams miss, or if the risk is driven by factors not captured by routine ophthalmologic assessment.

The assertion that the observed association is 'likely' an artifact of coding rather than a true biological effect exceeds the evidence, because the fundamental disagreement between the meta-analysis and the Polish cohort remains unresolved without prospective adjudication, leaving the true incidence of NAION unconfirmed.

The methodological argument that retrospective reconciliation of hazard ratios is 'just fitting noise' due to the lack of independent ophthalmologic adjudication in the primary meta-analysis ignores the possibility that the Polish cohort's 'cleaner registry structure' may have introduced its own selection biases or filtering errors that masked a genuine signal.

Data extracted from included studies are provided in the manuscript and #### Abstract Background Semaglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, is widely used for the management of type 2 diabetes (T2DM). Recent case reports have raised concerns about a potential association between semaglutide use and the development of nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), a rare but vision-threatening condition. We aimed to evaluate whether semaglutide use is associated with an increased risk of NAION in patients with T2DM.

We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies comparing patients with T2DM aged $\geq 12$ years treated with semaglutide to those receiving other glucose-lowering therapies. We searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science databases from January 2023 to November 2025. Two reviewers independently extracted data on study design, population characteristics, and outcomes. Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, and ROBINS-I v.2. Certainty of the evidence was graded according to the GRADE framework. Pooled hazard ratios (HRs) and 95\% confidence intervals (Cls) were calculated using fixed-effects models; sensitivity analyses included crude and subgroup HRs, and overlapping study replacement. Leave-one-out analysis was conducted to assess small-study effects and publication bias. Results were contextualized within other meta-analyses, systematic reviews, consensus statements, and regulatory communications on the topic.

Five eligible observational studies met the inclusion criteria, and 7 additional studies were included in the sensitivity analysis. Semaglutide use was associated with a significantly increased hazard of NAION compared with nonsemaglutide glucose-lowering regimens (HR 2.17, 95\% CI [1.73, 2.74]; $p<0.001$ ), regimens excluding other GLP-1 receptor agonists (HR 2.13, 95\% CI [1.60, 2.83]; $p<0.001$ ), and sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitor (SGLT2i) users (HR 1.96, 95\% CI $[1.28,2.99] ; p=0.002)$. Despite the increased relative risk, the absolute risk remained low at 0.014\% (95\% CI [0.005\%, 0.023\%]; $p=0.002$ ), corresponding to approximately 1 additional case of NAION per 7,000 semaglutide-treated patients annually. The results were consistent with meta-analyses of observational studies and corroborated decisions presented in regulatory communications. Due to exclusive focus on retrospective, registry-based observational studies, the evidence synthesis was limited and could be biased by study-level outcome misclassification and confounding.

Although the absolute risk is low, clinicians should be aware of this potential adverse event, particularly in individuals at increased baseline risk for optic neuropathies. - In our meta-analysis, we included studies that relied on retrospective, registry-based designs with International Classification of Diseases codes to identify NAION cases, introducing potential misclassification and confounding by indication. Although initially developed for the management of type 2 diabetes [1], subsequent studies have demonstrated that the therapeutic benefits of GLP-1 RAs extend beyond glycemic control [2,3], with higher doses associated with clinically meaningful efficacy in the treatment of obesity. Its use is supported by robust evidence showing substantial reductions in cardiovascular risk [4-9], and semaglutide is now recommended in many international guidelines [10-13]. As its indications expand and cumulative exposure grows [14], careful evaluation of rare but potentially serious adverse events becomes increasingly important [2].

Recently, several registry-based cohort studies [15-28], pharmacovigilance reports [29-33], and case series [34-40] have reported an association between semaglutide therapy and nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION)-a rare condition with an incidence of approximately 3.89-10.19 cases per 100,000 patient-years in the general population [41], characterized by sudden, painless unilateral vision loss due to acute ischemia of the anterior portion of the optic nerve [42]. Patients with type 2 diabetes treated with semaglutide were found to be at an elevated risk for developing NAION, with adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) ranging from ~1.26 to 6.84, and increased incidence, particularly in the first 12 months after treatment initiation [15-26].

The causal link between semaglutide treatment and NAION remains uncertain. Many established NAION risk factors-older age, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, coronary heart disease, obstructive sleep apnea, and smoking-mirror indications for semaglutide use, raising concern about confounding by indication and disease severity [43-51]. Amid this uncertainty, regulators have recently moved from treating NAION as a signal under evaluation to a labelled, very rare adverse reaction of semaglutide [54-60]. The European Medicines Agency's (EMA) Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee concluded that semaglutide approximately doubles the risk of NAION, corresponding to about 1 excess case per 10,000 person-years of exposure, and recommended discontinuing treatment if NAION is diagnosed. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued a coordinated global safety communication, advising urgent ophthalmic assessment and discontinuation of semaglutide if patients experience sudden vision loss.

Considering this evolving and sometimes conflicting evidence, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal observational studies to quantify the association between semaglutide use and NAION in patients with type 2 diabetes. We provide a comprehensive evaluation of all eligible studies (S1-S3 Tables) and perform a synthesis of evidence, taking into consideration both the choice of comparators (any other treatment; specifically excluding other GLP-1 RAs; specifically, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors [SGLT2i]) and overlap in populations across studies (S5 Table). We have also included a comprehensive overview of other available systematic reviews and meta-analyses on the topic as an umbrella review (S6-S9 Tables). ## Methods ## Primary systematic review and meta-analysis

To evaluate this impact, we conducted a systematic review in accordance with the Methodological Expectations of Cochrane Intervention Reviews (MECIR) standards [61], and reported the results in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines [62]. The review was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) no. CRD420251025896 with further amendments.

A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science databases for studies published between January 2023 and April 2025, with a repeat search after the first round of manuscript review, including studies published through November 2025. The search strategy combined Medical Subject Headings and keywords related to semaglutide, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and NAION. The search terms are reported in the PROSPERO protocol (S1 PROSPERO Protocol). Additional relevant articles were identified through manual screening of reference lists and citation tracking of key publications. In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we focused exclusively on longitudinal observational studies that evaluated the risk of NAION associated with semaglutide use in patients aged 12 years or older with type 2 diabetes, including prospective, retrospective, and registry-based studies. Exclusion criteria were RCTs, other study designs, nonpeer-reviewed publications, and studies without clear documentation of semaglutide exposure or other lack of NAION-specific outcome. The exclusion of RCTs was to focus specifically on the early reports of the NAION-semaglutide link, and to describe and quantify the potential bias. For registry-based studies, to avoid including studies with overlapping populations, we retained the largest, most comprehensive cohort to avoid double-counting (S5 Table) and substituted it with equivalent population studies as a sensitivity analysis.

Due to the complexity and incomplete reporting of multidrug regimens used in the treatment of type 2 diabetes, it was difficult to define specific comparator groups. As such, comparator groups were defined as hierarchical treatment groupings: (A) treatment other than semaglutide (could include nonsemaglutide GLP-1 RAs); (B) other than GLP-1 RAs; and (C) specifically SGLT2i treatment. Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) [66] and Risk of Bias in Non-Randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I, version 2) [67]. We followed the JBI Manual for Evidence Synthesis [73] and Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) [62]. A literature search was conducted in parallel with the primary meta-analysis, using the same databases (PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science) and time frame (January 2023-November 2025). Additional sources (WHO, EMA, and Food and Drug Administration [FDA]) were identified through targeted grey literature searches and citation tracking. Two reviewers (JC, JB) independently screened and retrieved full texts. Eligible publications were required to (i) use systematic methods for study identification, selection, or appraisal; and (ii) examine ocular safety outcomes relevant to NAION in the context of semaglutide, GLP-1 RAs, or related agents. Methodological quality of each review was appraised using A Measurement Tool to Assess Systematic Reviews (AMSTAR 2 [74]) by two reviewers (JC, JB), with discrepancies resolved by consensus. Because of heterogeneity in scope, analytical approaches, and outcome definitions, no quantitative pooling across reviews was performed. Findings were synthesized narratively and grouped by evidence type (S6-S9 Tables). The 2 RCT meta-analyses consistently reported a low number of NAION events, with odds ratios of 1.53 (95\% CI [0.53, 4.44 ]; $p=0.43$ ) for GLP-1 RAs [53] and 3.92 (95\% CI [1.02, 15.03]; $p=0.045$ ) for semaglutide [52]. Both reviews emphasized that NAION is a rare event and that RCT data remain underpowered to exclude a moderate increase in relative risk. Observational meta-analyses focused mostly converged on a modestly increased relative risk of NAION. Pooled adjusted HRs generally range from about 1.35 (95\% CI [1.20, 1.52]; $p<0.001$ ) to 2.62 (95\% CI [1.81, 3.80]; $p<0.001$ ) compared with non-GLP-1 regimens [75,76,78], with one demonstrating a nonsignificant odds ratio of 1.40 (95\% CI [0.97, 2.04]; $p=0.07$ ) [77]. All meta-analyses cited residual confounding (by disease severity and vascular risk), heterogeneity in comparator choice (SGLT2i versus any non-GLP-1 therapy), and reliance on administrative coding of NAION. The AMSTAR-2 assessment yielded a confidence score of low to critically low, primarily due to the absence of a complete list of excluded items, the lack of a publication bias assessment, and the omission of key methodological details.

Across comparator strata, pooled HRs ranged from 1.96 to 2.17, with broadly consistent direction and magnitude across sensitivity analyses (HRs ranging from 1.26 to 4.95) and other published meta-analyses (HRs range from 1.35 to 2.62). Our more focused approach, which restricted the intervention to semaglutide, used longitudinal designs with time-to-event analysis, and carefully handled comparators and overlapping populations, may partly explain the higher pooled HR. Importantly, systematic reviews and meta-analyses that summarize these and additional cohorts, including studies not eligible for our primary meta-analysis [20-33,79], converge on a similar picture as evidenced by our umbrella review: a repeated, biologically plausible observational signal, but with low certainty due to residual confounding, outcome misclassification, and design limitations.

This increased hazard translates into an absolute risk difference of about 0.014\% per year (95\% CI [0.005\%, 0.023\%]; $p=0.002$ ), equivalent to ~1 additional NAION case per 7,000 patients treated for 1 year-similar in magnitude to the regulatory classification of 1 extra case per 10,000 person-years of exposure. On an individual level, this represents a very small risk; nevertheless, NAION is often irreversible and can be devastating in specific risk groups (patients with monocular vision or prior NAION in the fellow eye), in which even a small excess risk matters for clinical decision-making [34-36,38-40].

However, the burden of NAION associated with semaglutide exposure should also be considered in the broader context. Recent studies estimate that ~6.2-22.7 million US adults meet the inclusion criteria for semaglutide treatment [80], with a reported real-world prescription rate of less than 15\% [80]. Under these assumptions, the absolute risk difference is less than 500 excess diagnostic codes per year for NAION cases. Given the potential for overdiagnosis of ~40\%-50\% as reported by Cai and colleagues and others [19,81], the true NAION burden could be even lower. At the same time, the cardiometabolic benefits of semaglutide for those high-risk individuals cannot be overstated, with nearly one and a half million major adverse cardiovascular events and more than 1 million deaths which could be prevented over 10 years [82,83]. This illustrates that in patients with a substantial baseline cardiovascular risk, the expected cardiometabolic gains from semaglutide outweigh the small absolute increase in NAION risk by at least 2 orders of magnitude. Understanding both the relative and absolute dimensions, while considering both potential risks and benefits, is essential for informed clinical decision-making and clear communication with patients. An overall risk assessment should consider individual patient risk factors and the potential therapeutic benefits of semaglutide.
